claim: The development and morphology of vascular plants is critically determined by synthesis and proper distribution of the phytohormone auxin.
source: The development and morphology of vascular plants is critically determined by synthesis and proper distribution of the phytohormone auxin.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of auxin in plant development.

claim: The directed cell-to-cell distribution of auxin is achieved through a system of auxin influx and efflux transporters.
source: The directed cell-to-cell distribution of auxin is achieved through a system of auxin influx and efflux transporters.
evidence: This is established knowledge about auxin transport mechanisms in plants.

claim: PIN-FORMED (PIN) proteins are proposed auxin efflux transporters.
source: PIN-FORMED (PIN) proteins are proposed auxin efflux transporters
evidence: This is a statement based on existing scientific literature about PIN protein function.

claim: PIN-mediated auxin transport is directly activated by D6 PROTEIN KINASE (D6PK) in a heterologous Xenopus oocyte system.
source: Here, we show in a heterologous Xenopus oocyte system as well as in Arabidopsis thaliana inflorescence stems that PIN-mediated auxin transport is directly activated by D6 PROTEIN KINASE (D6PK)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from oocyte auxin efflux assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: PIN-mediated auxin transport is directly activated by PINOID (PID)/WAG kinases in a heterologous Xenopus oocyte system.
source: Here, we show in a heterologous Xenopus oocyte system as well as in Arabidopsis thaliana inflorescence stems that PIN-mediated auxin transport is directly activated by D6 PROTEIN KINASE (D6PK) and PINOID (PID)/WAG kinases of the Arabidopsis AGCVIII kinase family.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from oocyte auxin efflux assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: PIN-mediated auxin transport is directly activated by D6PK in Arabidopsis thaliana inflorescence stems.
source: Here, we show in a heterologous Xenopus oocyte system as well as in Arabidopsis thaliana inflorescence stems that PIN-mediated auxin transport is directly activated by D6 PROTEIN KINASE (D6PK)
evidence: This claim is supported by auxin transport measurements in inflorescence stems of d6pk mutants.

claim: D6PKs and PID have differential phosphosite preferences.
source: At the same time, we reveal that D6PKs and PID have differential phosphosite preferences.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation experiments and mass spectrometry data showing different phosphorylation patterns.

claim: PIN activation by protein kinases is a crucial component of auxin transport control.
source: Our study suggests that PIN activation by protein kinases is a crucial component of auxin transport control that must be taken into account to understand auxin distribution within the plant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: AUXIN RESISTANT1 (AUX1)/LIKE-AUX1 (LAX) proteins are auxin influx transporters.
source: AUXIN RESISTANT1 (AUX1)/LIKE-AUX1 (LAX) proteins are auxin influx transporters and PIN-FORMED (PIN) proteins, which have been proposed to act in concert with ABC transporters, are the proposed auxin efflux transporters (Galweiler et al., 1998; Friml et al., 2002; Noh et al., 2003; Geisler et al., 2005; Bainbridge et al., 2008; Peret et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PIN proteins have been proposed to act in concert with ABC transporters as auxin efflux transporters.
source: AUXIN RESISTANT1 (AUX1)/LIKE-AUX1 (LAX) proteins are auxin influx transporters and PIN-FORMED (PIN) proteins, which have been proposed to act in concert with ABC transporters, are the proposed auxin efflux transporters (Galweiler et al., 1998; Friml et al., 2002; Noh et al., 2003; Geisler et al., 2005; Bainbridge et al., 2008; Peret et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The directed transport of auxin throughout the plant is critically determined by the asymmetric plasma membrane distribution of PINs in many cells.
source: The directed transport of auxin throughout the plant is critically determined by the—in many cells–asymmetric plasma membrane distribution of PINs and plant developmental processes have been successfully modeled based on the knowledge of PIN distribution and PIN protein behavior (Jonsson et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2006; Wisniewska et al., 2006; Blakeslee et al., 2007; Grieneisen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Plant developmental processes have been successfully modeled based on the knowledge of PIN distribution and PIN protein behavior.
source: The directed transport of auxin throughout the plant is critically determined by the—in many cells–asymmetric plasma membrane distribution of PINs and plant developmental processes have been successfully modeled based on the knowledge of PIN distribution and PIN protein behavior (Jonsson et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2006; Wisniewska et al., 2006; Blakeslee et al., 2007; Grieneisen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The D6PK family is comprised of four functionally redundant members: D6PK, D6PK-LIKE1 (D6PKL1), D6PKL2 and D6PKL3.
source: The D6PK family is comprised of four functionally redundant members, namely D6PK, D6PK-LIKE1 (D6PKL1), D6PKL2 and D6PKL3.
evidence: This is a statement about the composition of the D6PK family based on previous research.

claim: D6PKs colocalize with PIN proteins at the basal (rootward) plasma membrane in cells of the root cortex and stele.
source: Although D6PKs are devoid of any sequence features indicative for an association of these protein kinases with the plasma membrane, D6PKs colocalize with PIN proteins at the basal (rootward) plasma membrane in cells of the root cortex and stele, the hypocotyl and main inflorescence stem as well as the shoot apical meristem (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: D6PKs colocalize with PIN proteins at the basal plasma membrane in cells of the hypocotyl.
source: Although D6PKs are devoid of any sequence features indicative for an association of these protein kinases with the plasma membrane, D6PKs colocalize with PIN proteins at the basal (rootward) plasma membrane in cells of the root cortex and stele, the hypocotyl and main inflorescence stem as well as the shoot apical meristem (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: D6PKs colocalize with PIN proteins at the basal plasma membrane in cells of the main inflorescence stem.
source: Although D6PKs are devoid of any sequence features indicative for an association of these protein kinases with the plasma membrane, D6PKs colocalize with PIN proteins at the basal (rootward) plasma membrane in cells of the root cortex and stele, the hypocotyl and main inflorescence stem as well as the shoot apical meristem (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: D6PKs colocalize with PIN proteins at the basal plasma membrane in cells of the shoot apical meristem.
source: Although D6PKs are devoid of any sequence features indicative for an association of these protein kinases with the plasma membrane, D6PKs colocalize with PIN proteins at the basal (rootward) plasma membrane in cells of the root cortex and stele, the hypocotyl and main inflorescence stem as well as the shoot apical meristem (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: D6PKs phosphorylate PIN proteins in vitro.
source: D6PKs phosphorylate PIN proteins in vitro and PIN phosphorylation is reduced in d6pk mutants in vivo without affecting PIN distribution or strongly affecting PIN abundance (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Willige et al., 2013; Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PIN phosphorylation is reduced in d6pk mutants in vivo.
source: D6PKs phosphorylate PIN proteins in vitro and PIN phosphorylation is reduced in d6pk mutants in vivo without affecting PIN distribution or strongly affecting PIN abundance (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Willige et al., 2013; Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Loss of D6PK function does not affect PIN distribution.
source: D6PKs phosphorylate PIN proteins in vitro and PIN phosphorylation is reduced in d6pk mutants in vivo without affecting PIN distribution or strongly affecting PIN abundance (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Willige et al., 2013; Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Loss of D6PK function does not strongly affect PIN abundance.
source: D6PKs phosphorylate PIN proteins in vitro and PIN phosphorylation is reduced in d6pk mutants in vivo without affecting PIN distribution or strongly affecting PIN abundance (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Willige et al., 2013; Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PINs and D6PK constitutively cycle intracellularly between endosomal compartments and the plasma membrane.
source: Just as the PINs, D6PK constitutively cycles intracellularly between endosomal compartments and the plasma membrane but both, PINs and D6PK, traffic via distinct intracellular routes and seemingly encounter each other only at the basal plasma membrane (Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PINs and D6PK traffic via distinct intracellular routes.
source: Just as the PINs, D6PK constitutively cycles intracellularly between endosomal compartments and the plasma membrane but both, PINs and D6PK, traffic via distinct intracellular routes and seemingly encounter each other only at the basal plasma membrane (Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PINs and D6PK seemingly encounter each other only at the basal plasma membrane.
source: Just as the PINs, D6PK constitutively cycles intracellularly between endosomal compartments and the plasma membrane but both, PINs and D6PK, traffic via distinct intracellular routes and seemingly encounter each other only at the basal plasma membrane (Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PIN phosphorylation rapidly reacts to the presence and absence of D6PK at the plasma membrane.
source: Since PIN phosphorylation, as assessed by evaluating overall PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation levels, rapidly reacts to the presence and absence of D6PK at the plasma membrane, we postulated that D6PKs directly activate auxin transport by PIN phosphorylation (Willige et al., 2013; Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The AGCVIII kinase subfamily comprises the proteins PINOID (PID), WAG1, and WAG2.
source: Another subfamily of AGCVIII kinases comprises the proteins PINOID (PID), WAG1, and WAG2 (Christensen et al., 2000; Benjamins et al., 2001; Santner and Watson, 2006; Galvan-Ampudia and Offringa, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of PINs by PID/WAGs has previously been proposed to control PIN polarity.
source: Phosphorylation of PINs by PID/WAGs has previously been proposed to control PIN polarity (Friml et al., 2004; Michniewicz et al., 2007; Dhonukshe et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PID/WAGs phosphorylate PINs at three highly conserved phosphosites, designated S1–S3.
source: PID/WAGs phosphorylate PINs at three highly conserved phosphosites, designated S1–S3 (Dhonukshe et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Modulating PIN phosphorylation by PID or WAG overexpression results in a basal-to-apical shift in PIN polar distribution.
source: Modulating PIN phosphorylation either by PID or WAG overexpression or by introducing phosphorylation-mimicking mutants in PIN1 seemingly results in a basal-to-apical shift in PIN polar distribution (Michniewicz et al., 2007; Dhonukshe et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Introducing phosphorylation-mimicking mutants in PIN1 results in a basal-to-apical shift in PIN polar distribution.
source: Modulating PIN phosphorylation either by PID or WAG overexpression or by introducing phosphorylation-mimicking mutants in PIN1 seemingly results in a basal-to-apical shift in PIN polar distribution (Michniewicz et al., 2007; Dhonukshe et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: pin1 mutants have a pin-formed inflorescence because they are devoid of the central auxin efflux protein required for shoot meristem differentiation.
source: pin1 mutants, on the one side, have a pin-formed inflorescence because they are devoid of the central auxin efflux protein required for shoot meristem differentiation (Galweiler et al., 1998)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: pid mutants are deficient in PIN1 phosphorylation.
source: pid mutants, on the other side, are deficient in PIN1 phosphorylation, which seemingly prevents the essential basal-to-apical polarity switch required to redirect auxin fluxes during differentiation at the shoot meristem (Friml et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The PID/WAG-mediated repolarization of PIN proteins is important for phototropic responses.
source: The PID/WAG-mediated repolarization of PIN proteins is also important for phototropic responses (Ding et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: During phototropic bending of the hypocotyl, the polarity of PIN3 protein changes upon light exposure.
source: During phototropic bending of the hypocotyl, the polarity of the relevant PIN3 protein changes upon light exposure and this polarity switch is required for auxin redistribution in the hypocotyl and for efficient phototropism.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PIN3 behavior during phototropism.

claim: PIN3 polarity change is required for auxin redistribution in the hypocotyl and for efficient phototropism.
source: During phototropic bending of the hypocotyl, the polarity of the relevant PIN3 protein changes upon light exposure and this polarity switch is required for auxin redistribution in the hypocotyl and for efficient phototropism.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PIN3 function in phototropism.

claim: PIN3 polarity change requires the activity of PID/WAG protein kinases.
source: This PIN3 polarity change requires the activity of PID/WAG protein kinases and it has been proposed that PID/WAG-dependent PIN3 phosphorylations directly control this process (Ding et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: d6pk mutants are strongly impaired in phototropic hypocotyl bending.
source: We showed previously that D6PKs also play a critical role in this process: d6pk mutants are strongly impaired in phototropic hypocotyl bending and the inability of d6pk mutants to efficiently transport auxin from the cotyledons to the hypocotyl may be responsible for this tropism defect (Willige et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The inability of d6pk mutants to efficiently transport auxin from the cotyledons to the hypocotyl may be responsible for the phototropism defect.
source: We showed previously that D6PKs also play a critical role in this process: d6pk mutants are strongly impaired in phototropic hypocotyl bending and the inability of d6pk mutants to efficiently transport auxin from the cotyledons to the hypocotyl may be responsible for this tropism defect (Willige et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism underlying the phototropism defect.

claim: The light-induced and PID/WAG-dependent PIN3 polarity changes can still take place in the absence of D6PKs.
source: Importantly, the light-induced and PID/WAG-dependent PIN3 polarity changes required for hypocotyl bending can still take place in the absence of D6PKs suggesting that the function of PID/WAGs in auxin transport and phototropism can be uncoupled from that of the D6PKs and that both kinases may control PINs independently and differentially (Willige et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The function of PID/WAGs in auxin transport and phototropism can be uncoupled from that of the D6PKs.
source: Importantly, the light-induced and PID/WAG-dependent PIN3 polarity changes required for hypocotyl bending can still take place in the absence of D6PKs suggesting that the function of PID/WAGs in auxin transport and phototropism can be uncoupled from that of the D6PKs and that both kinases may control PINs independently and differentially (Willige et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PIN3 polarity changes occur in d6pk mutants.

claim: D6PKs and PID/WAGs may control PINs independently and differentially.
source: Importantly, the light-induced and PID/WAG-dependent PIN3 polarity changes required for hypocotyl bending can still take place in the absence of D6PKs suggesting that the function of PID/WAGs in auxin transport and phototropism can be uncoupled from that of the D6PKs and that both kinases may control PINs independently and differentially (Willige et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PIN3 polarity changes occur in d6pk mutants.

claim: The overexpression of PID and WAG kinases results in a basal-to-apical PIN shift.
source: While the overexpression of PID and WAG kinases results in a basal-to-apical PIN shift, the overexpression of D6PKs does not affect PIN distribution (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Dhonukshe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The overexpression of D6PKs does not affect PIN distribution.
source: While the overexpression of PID and WAG kinases results in a basal-to-apical PIN shift, the overexpression of D6PKs does not affect PIN distribution (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Dhonukshe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The loss of PID function results in strong differentiation defects of the primary inflorescence.
source: Inversely, the loss of PID function results in strong differentiation defects of the primary inflorescence, which are not apparent in the d6pk mutants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pid mutant phenotypes.

claim: Strong differentiation defects of the primary inflorescence are not apparent in d6pk mutants.
source: Inversely, the loss of PID function results in strong differentiation defects of the primary inflorescence, which are not apparent in the d6pk mutants.
evidence: This is a statement about the phenotype of d6pk mutants.

claim: Basipetal auxin transport is reduced in inflorescence stems of d6pk mutants.
source: We showed that basipetal auxin transport was reduced in inflorescence stems of d6pk mutants
evidence: This claim is supported by auxin transport measurements presented in Figure 1.

claim: Auxin transport is as strongly impaired in the d6pk012 triple mutant as in mutants of PIN1.
source: While auxin transport defects were comparatively subtle in d6pk single mutants, the decrease in basipetal auxin transport was as strongly impaired in the d6pk012 triple mutant as in mutants of PIN1, a major PIN protein in this tissue (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by auxin transport measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: D6PKs are coexpressed with PINs in stems.
source: Furthermore, we found that D6PKs are coexpressed with PINs in stems (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by GUS reporter staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: D6PK and PIN1 localize to the basal plasma membrane in cells where auxin levels are high.
source: and that both, D6PK and PIN1, localize to the basal plasma membrane in cells where auxin levels are high as suggested by the auxin response reporter DR5:GFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: D6PKs have an essential role in auxin transport regulation in inflorescence stems.
source: Based on these observations, we concluded that D6PKs have an essential role in auxin transport regulation in inflorescence stems.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the auxin transport and localization data.

claim: PIN1 and PIN3 are unable to promote auxin efflux in the Xenopus oocyte system in the absence of exogenous protein kinases.
source: Interestingly, when we tested PIN1 or PIN3 alone, we did not observe any measurable auxin efflux that differed from the background, suggesting that the PINs are inactive auxin transporters in the oocyte system.
evidence: This claim is supported by auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Co-expression of D6PK with PIN1 or PIN3 results in significant and kinase activity-dependent activation of auxin efflux in oocytes.
source: However, when we co-expressed D6PK with the PINs we observed a significant and kinase activity-dependent activation of auxin efflux.
evidence: This claim is supported by auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: D6PK activation of PIN-mediated auxin efflux correlates with the appearance of high molecular weight bands for PIN1 and PIN3 in anti-PIN immunoblots.
source: This activation correlated with the appearance of high molecular weight bands for PIN1 and PIN3 that appeared in anti-PIN immunoblots only in the presence of the active D6PK kinase (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A kinase-dead variant of D6PK cannot activate auxin efflux in the oocyte system.
source: In line with an activation of PINs by D6PK through direct PIN phosphorylation, a kinase-dead variant of D6PK could not activate auxin efflux in this system (Figure 2D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 2D and 2F.

claim: D6PK is an activator of PIN-mediated auxin efflux in the oocyte expression system.
source: In summary, these experiments showed that D6PK is an activator of PIN-mediated auxin efflux in the oocyte expression system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the oocyte auxin efflux experiments.

claim: D6PK phosphorylates PIN1, PIN2, PIN3, and PIN4 at specific phosphosites including two novel serine residues designated S4 and S5.
source: Using mass spectrometry, we next identified D6PK-dependent phosphosites in the PINs after in vitro phosphorylation of the cytoplasmic loops (CL) of PIN1, PIN2, PIN3 and PIN4. These analyses resulted in the identification of two novel serine residues as conserved PIN phosphosites, S4 and S5, as well as three further serine phosphosites, S1–S3, that had previously been identified as phosphosites of the PID/WAG kinases (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—source data 1; Dhonukshe et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3 and related supplements.

claim: S1, S2 and S3 are conserved in PIN1, PIN2, PIN3, and PIN4.
source: Whereas S1, S2 and S3 are conserved in all four PINs tested, S4 and S5 are not conserved in PIN2 where the corresponding protein sequence motifs are divergent when compared to PIN1, PIN3, PIN4 and PIN7 and when compared to the strong conservation of the S1–S3 phosphosites in all PINs including PIN2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: S4 and S5 are not conserved in PIN2.
source: Whereas S1, S2 and S3 are conserved in all four PINs tested, S4 and S5 are not conserved in PIN2 where the corresponding protein sequence motifs are divergent when compared to PIN1, PIN3, PIN4 and PIN7 and when compared to the strong conservation of the S1–S3 phosphosites in all PINs including PIN2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: S5 is not conserved in PIN1 but aligns with a strongly conserved region of PIN1 at position D215.
source: Furthermore, S5 was not conserved in PIN1 but aligned with a strongly conserved region of PIN1. At the position of S5, PIN1 had an aspartic acid (D; D215) and we speculated that D215 might be a natural phosphomimic variant of the S5 site (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A synthetic peptide comprising PIN1 D215S can be phosphorylated by D6PK in vitro.
source: Indeed, while a synthetic peptide comprising PIN1 D215 could not be phosphorylated by D6PK in vitro, the D215S peptide variant was efficiently phosphorylated indicating that, although the respective S5 phosphosite was not conserved, the sequence conservation in this region was sufficient for phosphorylation by D6PK.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation experiments with synthetic peptides shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A synthetic peptide comprising PIN1 D215 cannot be phosphorylated by D6PK in vitro.
source: Indeed, while a synthetic peptide comprising PIN1 D215 could not be phosphorylated by D6PK in vitro, the D215S peptide variant was efficiently phosphorylated
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation experiments with synthetic peptides shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PIN2-specific peptides corresponding to the S4 or S5 phosphosites cannot be phosphorylated by D6PK.
source: In contrast, PIN2-specific peptides corresponding to the S4 or S5 phosphosites could not be phosphorylated by D6PK despite the fact that their sequences also contained serine residues.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation experiments with synthetic peptides shown in Figure 3B.

claim: S4 and S5 are novel PIN protein phosphosites that are differentially conserved in the five plasma membrane-resident PIN proteins.
source: Thus, S4 and S5 are novel PIN protein phosphosites that are differentially conserved in the five plasma membrane-resident PIN proteins with a role in promoting auxin efflux.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phosphorylation and sequence analysis data.

claim: PIN1 CL phosphorylation by D6PK is strongly reduced (40% of wild type levels) in a PIN1 S4A mutant.
source: When we examined the contribution of the individual phosphosites to PIN1 phosphorylation in the context of the PIN1 cytoplasmic loop (CL) fragment, we found that PIN1 CL phosphorylation by D6PK was already strongly reduced (40% of wild type levels) in a mutant variant where only PIN1 S4 was replaced by an alanine (S4A; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutations of PIN1 S1, PIN1 S2 or PIN1 S3 alone impair phosphorylation by D6PK to a lesser extent (ca. 80%).
source: In turn, mutations of the phosphosites PIN1 S1, PIN1 S2 or PIN1 S3 alone impaired phosphorylation by D6PK to a lesser extent (ca. 80%) and only mutation of all three sites in PIN1 S1A S2A S3A led to a clear reduction of PIN1 CL phosphorylation (58%; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutation of all three sites PIN1 S1A S2A S3A leads to a clear reduction of PIN1 CL phosphorylation (58%).
source: In turn, mutations of the phosphosites PIN1 S1, PIN1 S2 or PIN1 S3 alone impaired phosphorylation by D6PK to a lesser extent (ca. 80%) and only mutation of all three sites in PIN1 S1A S2A S3A led to a clear reduction of PIN1 CL phosphorylation (58%; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The mutation of all four PIN1 phosphosites in PIN1 S1A S2A S3A S4A abolishes phosphorylation by D6PK almost completely (2.7%).
source: Finally, the mutation of all four PIN1 phosphosites under investigation in PIN1 S1A S2A S3A S4A abolished phosphorylation by D6PK almost completely (2.7%; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: S4 is a major phosphosite for D6PK in PIN1.
source: Based on these analyses, we concluded that S4 is a major phosphosite for D6PK in PIN1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro phosphorylation data.

claim: The phosphorylation of PIN1 CL by PID is not altered in the PIN1 S4A mutant when compared to the wild type (100%).
source: In the case of PID, the phosphorylation of PIN1 CL by PID was not altered in the PIN1 S4A mutant when compared to the wild type (100%; 40% for D6PK) but already strongly affected by the PIN1 S1A mutation (61%; ca. 80% for D6PK) and even more by PIN1 S1A S2A S3A (18%; 58% for D6PK; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The phosphorylation of PIN1 CL by PID is strongly affected by the PIN1 S1A mutation (61%).
source: In the case of PID, the phosphorylation of PIN1 CL by PID was not altered in the PIN1 S4A mutant when compared to the wild type (100%; 40% for D6PK) but already strongly affected by the PIN1 S1A mutation (61%; ca. 80% for D6PK) and even more by PIN1 S1A S2A S3A (18%; 58% for D6PK; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The phosphorylation of PIN1 CL by PID is even more affected by PIN1 S1A S2A S3A (18%).
source: In the case of PID, the phosphorylation of PIN1 CL by PID was not altered in the PIN1 S4A mutant when compared to the wild type (100%; 40% for D6PK) but already strongly affected by the PIN1 S1A mutation (61%; ca. 80% for D6PK) and even more by PIN1 S1A S2A S3A (18%; 58% for D6PK; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: D6PK and PID have an overlapping but also differential preference for specific phosphosites in PIN1.
source: Thus, D6PK and PID have an overlapping but also differential preference for specific phosphosites in PIN1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative in vitro phosphorylation data.

claim: A PIN3 CL S4A S5A variant is still efficiently phosphorylated by PID.
source: Whereas a PIN3 CL S4A S5A variant was still efficiently phosphorylated by PID its phosphorylation by D6PK was severely impaired (28%; Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Phosphorylation of PIN3 CL S4A S5A by D6PK is severely impaired (28%).
source: Whereas a PIN3 CL S4A S5A variant was still efficiently phosphorylated by PID its phosphorylation by D6PK was severely impaired (28%; Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Mutations of the five phosphosites have differential effects in the case of D6PK or PID.
source: Thus, mutations of the five phosphosites have differential effects in the case of D6PK or PID.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative in vitro phosphorylation data.

claim: A PIN1 S4A mutant is significantly impaired in auxin efflux activation by D6PK in oocytes.
source: In line with the proposed important role of S4 for PIN1 phosphorylation, we found that a PIN1 S4A mutant was already significantly impaired in auxin efflux activation by D6PK in the auxin efflux experiments (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The requirement of PIN1 S1, S2, and S3 for D6PK activation is not obvious with a PIN1 S1A S2A S3A mutant but becomes apparent in the presence of the S4A mutation.
source: At the same time, the requirement of PIN1 S1, S2, and S3 for D6PK activation was not obvious with a PIN1 S1A S2A S3A mutant but became apparent in the presence of the S4A mutation where the PIN1 activation defect of the S4A mutation was further enhanced in the presence of mutations of the other three sites (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PIN1 S4 is an important site for D6PK-dependent PIN1 activation but all four phosphosites are required for full PIN1 activation.
source: We thus concluded that PIN1 S4 is an important site for D6PK-dependent PIN1 activation but that all four phosphosites are required for full PIN1 activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the oocyte auxin efflux assay data.

claim: A PIN3 S4A S5A variant shows reduced responsiveness to D6PK when compared to wild type PIN3.
source: Also, in line with the results obtained in the in vitro phosphorylation experiments, we found that a PIN3 S4A S5A variant showed reduced responsiveness to D6PK when compared to wild type PIN3 providing further support for the importance of the S4 and S5 phosphosites for PIN activation by D6PK (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The auxin efflux activation of wild type PIN1 protein is indistinguishable from the behavior of the PIN1 D215S mutant in oocyte experiments.
source: However, we found that the auxin efflux (activation) of the wild type PIN1 protein was indistinguishable from the behavior of the PIN1 D215S mutant in these oocyte experiments (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The auxin transport defect in inflorescence stems of pin1 mutants is only partially rescued by PIN1 S4A compared to a full rescue with wild type PIN1.
source: In support of an important but not exclusive role of S4 phosphorylation for PIN1 function, we detected only a partial rescue of the auxin transport defect in inflorescence stems of pin1 mutants transformed with PIN1 S4A compared to a full rescue with the wild type PIN1.
evidence: This claim is supported by auxin transport measurements in inflorescence stems shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The PIN1 S4A mutant and wild type PIN1 transgene are able to complement the PID-dependent inflorescence differentiation defect of the pin1 mutant.
source: While the mutant and the wild type transgene were able to complement the PID-dependent inflorescence differentiation defect of the pin1 mutant (Figure 6C,D), D6PK-dependent basipetal auxin transport in the stem was compromised (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: D6PK-dependent basipetal auxin transport in the stem is compromised in pin1 mutants expressing PIN1 S4A.
source: While the mutant and the wild type transgene were able to complement the PID-dependent inflorescence differentiation defect of the pin1 mutant (Figure 6C,D), D6PK-dependent basipetal auxin transport in the stem was compromised (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by auxin transport measurements shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: PIN1 S4A shows an identical behavior to wild type PIN1 in BFA sensitivity experiments.
source: Since PIN1 S4A showed an identical behavior to wild type PIN1 in these experiments, we concluded that changes in PIN1 polarity, PIN1 trafficking or PIN1 abundance at the plasma membrane may not be causal for the observed differences in basipetal auxin transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes in PIN1 polarity, PIN1 trafficking or PIN1 abundance at the plasma membrane may not be causal for the observed differences in basipetal auxin transport in PIN1 S4A.
source: Since PIN1 S4A showed an identical behavior to wild type PIN1 in these experiments, we concluded that changes in PIN1 polarity, PIN1 trafficking or PIN1 abundance at the plasma membrane may not be causal for the observed differences in basipetal auxin transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BFA sensitivity and localization experiments.

claim: The phototropism defect of the pin347 mutant is only partially complemented by the PIN3 S4A S5A transgene.
source: When we measured the ability of wild type PIN3 and mutant PIN3 S4A S5A to complement the pin347 mutant when expressed from a PIN3 promoter fragment, we found that the phototropism defect of the pin347 mutant was only partially complemented by the PIN3 S4A S5A transgene while it was fully complemented by wild type PIN3 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by phototropism measurements shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The phototropism defect of the pin347 mutant is fully complemented by wild type PIN3.
source: When we measured the ability of wild type PIN3 and mutant PIN3 S4A S5A to complement the pin347 mutant when expressed from a PIN3 promoter fragment, we found that the phototropism defect of the pin347 mutant was only partially complemented by the PIN3 S4A S5A transgene while it was fully complemented by wild type PIN3 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by phototropism measurements shown in Figure 6E.

claim: D6PK-dependent PIN3 S4 and S5 phosphorylations are required for efficient basipetal auxin transport in the hypocotyls of dark-grown seedlings.
source: This finding was in line with the hypothesis that D6PK-dependent PIN3 S4 and S5 phosphorylations are required for efficient basipetal auxin transport in the hypocotyls of dark-grown seedlings, which is a prerequisite for efficient hypocotyl bending.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the partial complementation of the phototropism defect by PIN3 S4A S5A.

claim: The mutation of the PIN3 S1–S3 phosphosites fully impairs the ability of the PIN3 transgene to complement the pin347 mutation.
source: Consistent with the predominant role of the PID phosphosite phosphorylation at S1–S3, we found that the mutation of the PIN3 S1–S3 phosphosites as well as mutation of all five PIN3 phosphosites, S1–S5, fully impaired the ability of the PIN3 transgene to complement the pin347 mutation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by phototropism measurements shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The mutation of all five PIN3 phosphosites, S1–S5, fully impairs the ability of the PIN3 transgene to complement the pin347 mutation.
source: Consistent with the predominant role of the PID phosphosite phosphorylation at S1–S3, we found that the mutation of the PIN3 S1–S3 phosphosites as well as mutation of all five PIN3 phosphosites, S1–S5, fully impaired the ability of the PIN3 transgene to complement the pin347 mutation (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by phototropism measurements shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The novel phosphosites, PIN3 S4 and S5, are required for full PIN3 activity, most likely by interfering primarily with basipetal auxin transport in the hypocotyls of dark-grown seedlings.
source: In summary, this experiment supported the conclusion that the novel phosphosites, PIN3 S4 and S5, are required for full PIN3 activity, most likely by interfering primarily with basipetal auxin transport in the hypocotyls of dark-grown seedlings.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phototropism complementation experiments.

claim: Phosphorylation at PIN1 S4 is strongly reduced in the d6pk012 triple mutant.
source: In these experiments, we detected a strong reduction in the in vivo abundance of the PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 phosphorylations that increased with increasing d6pk mutant complexity (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Phosphorylation at PIN3 S4 is strongly reduced in the d6pk012 triple mutant.
source: In these experiments, we detected a strong reduction in the in vivo abundance of the PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 phosphorylations that increased with increasing d6pk mutant complexity (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The decrease in S4 phosphorylation cannot be explained by changes in the overall abundance of PIN proteins.
source: This decrease in S4 phosphorylation could not be explained by changes in the overall abundance of PIN proteins as shown by quantitative SRM analyses of the unphosphorylated PIN1 and PIN3 S4 peptides and analyses of internal control peptides (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Introducing a D6PK transgene expressing D6PK under control of a D6PK promoter fragment rescues the PIN1 and PIN3 S4 phosphorylation defects.
source: Furthermore, introducing a D6PK transgene expressing D6PK under control of a D6PK promoter fragment rescued the PIN1 and PIN3 S4 phosphorylation defects (Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The abundance of phosphorylation at PIN3 S5 is as strongly reduced in the d6pk012 triple mutant as observed for the S4 site.
source: We also examined phosphorylation at PIN3 S5 using the same methodology and observed that the abundance of phosphorylation at these sites was as strongly reduced in the d6pk012 triple mutant as observed for the S4 site.
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The phosphorylation defect at PIN3 S5 is rescued by a D6PK transgene.
source: Again, the phosphorylation defect could not be explained by changes in PIN3 abundance and was rescued by a D6PK transgene as described above (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The observed decreases in PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation are in good agreement with the reductions in auxin transport detected in the same tissue of d6pk mutants.
source: Most importantly, the observed decreases in PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation were in good agreement with the reductions in auxin transport that we had detected in the same tissue of d6pk mutants (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a comparison of the phosphorylation data with the auxin transport data.

claim: D6PKs are the major kinases targeting PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4, and PIN3 S5 in Arabidopsis inflorescence stems.
source: We therefore concluded that D6PKs are the major kinases targeting PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4, and PIN3 S5 in Arabidopsis inflorescence stems and that the reduced phosphorylation at these sites may be causal for the reduced auxin transport of d6pk mutants in this tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis data.

claim: The reduced phosphorylation at PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4, and PIN3 S5 may be causal for the reduced auxin transport of d6pk mutants in inflorescence stems.
source: We therefore concluded that D6PKs are the major kinases targeting PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4, and PIN3 S5 in Arabidopsis inflorescence stems and that the reduced phosphorylation at these sites may be causal for the reduced auxin transport of d6pk mutants in this tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis and auxin transport data.

claim: PID and WAG2 are able to activate PIN1-mediated auxin efflux in oocytes.
source: Interestingly, PID and WAG2 but not phot1 or UCN were able to activate PIN1-mediated auxin efflux (Figure 8A,B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 8A, 8B, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: phot1 and UCN are not able to activate PIN1-mediated auxin efflux in oocytes.
source: Interestingly, PID and WAG2 but not phot1 or UCN were able to activate PIN1-mediated auxin efflux (Figure 8A,B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: PID and WAG2 have a role in PIN activation besides their previously reported role in the control of PIN polarity.
source: We thus concluded that PID and WAG2 have a role in PIN activation besides their previously reported role in the control of PIN polarity (Friml et al., 2004; Dhonukshe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the oocyte auxin efflux assay data.

claim: The PIN1 S1A S2A S3A mutant is less efficiently activated by PID than by D6PK.
source: Indeed, we found, in agreement with the in vitro data, that the PIN1 S1A S2A S3A mutant was less efficiently activated by PID than by D6PK (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The PIN1 S4A mutation does not significantly affect activation by PID.
source: Inversely, the PIN1 S4A mutation that strongly affected activation by D6PK did not significantly affect activation by PID.
evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Mutation of all four PIN1 phosphosites, PIN1 S1A–S4A, results in the strongest impairment of PIN1 activation by PID.
source: Again, mutation of all four PIN1 phosphosites, PIN1 S1A–S4A, resulted in the strongest impairment of PIN1 activation by PID (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Neither pid nor wag1 wag2 mutants show a clear reduction in PIN S4 phosphorylation.
source: However, in contrast to the strong defects in PIN S4 phosphorylation that we observed in the d6pk mutants, neither pid nor wag1 wag2 mutants showed a clear reduction in PIN phosphorylation at the S4 phosphosite suggesting that PID and WAG1/WAG2 do not contribute to PIN S4 phosphorylation in this tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: PID and WAG1/WAG2 do not contribute to PIN S4 phosphorylation in inflorescence stems.
source: However, in contrast to the strong defects in PIN S4 phosphorylation that we observed in the d6pk mutants, neither pid nor wag1 wag2 mutants showed a clear reduction in PIN phosphorylation at the S4 phosphosite suggesting that PID and WAG1/WAG2 do not contribute to PIN S4 phosphorylation in this tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis data.

claim: The phosphorylation at the S1 phosphosites is not affected when comparing the d6pk012 mutant with the d6pk012 mutant expressing a complementing D6PK transgene.
source: Our analysis of PIN1 and PIN3 S1 phosphorylations, however, showed that the phosphorylation at the S1 phosphosites was not affected when comparing the d6pk012 mutant with the d6pk012 mutant expressing a complementing D6PK transgene suggesting that D6PK does not contribute to the phosphorylation of S1 in vivo (Figure 8—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: D6PK does not contribute to the phosphorylation of S1 in vivo.
source: Our analysis of PIN1 and PIN3 S1 phosphorylations, however, showed that the phosphorylation at the S1 phosphosites was not affected when comparing the d6pk012 mutant with the d6pk012 mutant expressing a complementing D6PK transgene suggesting that D6PK does not contribute to the phosphorylation of S1 in vivo (Figure 8—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis data.

claim: D6PK and PID cannot functionally replace each other when expressed from the promoter of the respective other gene.
source: These experiments demonstrated that D6PK and PID cannot functionally replace each other when expressed from the promoter of the respective other gene (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic complementation experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: The expression of PID from a PID promoter fragment is sufficient to complement the phenotypes of a pid mutant.
source: Whereas the expression of PID from a PID promoter fragment was sufficient to complement the phenotypes of a pid mutant, the expression of D6PK under control of the PID promoter fragment failed to complement pid (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic complementation experiments shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The expression of D6PK under control of the PID promoter fragment fails to complement pid.
source: Whereas the expression of PID from a PID promoter fragment was sufficient to complement the phenotypes of a pid mutant, the expression of D6PK under control of the PID promoter fragment failed to complement pid (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic complementation experiments shown in Figure 9A.

claim: D6PK expression from a D6PK promoter fragment is sufficient to complement the d6pk012 mutant.
source: Inversely, D6PK but not PID expression from a D6PK promoter fragment was sufficient to complement the d6pk012 mutant (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic complementation experiments shown in Figure 9B.

claim: PID expression from a D6PK promoter fragment is not sufficient to complement the d6pk012 mutant.
source: Inversely, D6PK but not PID expression from a D6PK promoter fragment was sufficient to complement the d6pk012 mutant (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic complementation experiments shown in Figure 9B.

claim: D6PK and PID/WAGs are functionally divergent.
source: In summary, these genetic experiments supported our conclusion that D6PK and PID/WAGs are functionally divergent and these findings and conclusions are in line with previous observations on the differential effects of these two kinases in PIN polarity control (Dhonukshe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic complementation experiments.

claim: Differential phosphosite preferences may be the basis of the distinct roles of D6PK and PID/WAGs in the control of PIN polarity and plant growth control.
source: These differential phosophosite preferences as detected in in vitro as well as in vivo phosphosite analyses may be the basis of the distinct roles of the two kinases in the control of PIN polarity and plant growth control.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the molecular basis of functional differences.

claim: Concentration-, time- and D6PK-dependent increases in the phosphorylation of PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4 and PIN3 S5 occur already 15 min after auxin application.
source: In these analyses, we detected concentration-, time- and D6PK-dependent increases in the phosphorylation of PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4 and PIN3 S5 already 15 min after auxin application (Figure 10A,B, Figure 10—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 10 and related supplements.

claim: Only marginal increases in PIN phosphorylation at S4 and S5 are observed in the phosphorylation deficient d6pk012 mutant after auxin treatment.
source: While these increases were clearly observed in the wild type, only marginal increases in PIN phosphorylation at these sites were observed in the phosphorylation deficient d6pk012 mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 10 and related supplements.

claim: Phosphorylation at the preferential PID target site S1 is neither strongly impaired in d6pk012 mutants nor clearly induced by auxin.
source: At the same time, phosphorylation at the preferential PID target site S1 was neither strongly impaired in d6pk012 mutants when compared to a d6pk012 mutant expressing a complementing D6PK transgene nor clearly induced by auxin (Figure 8—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: Increased phosphorylation at S4 and S5 is detected in the auxin-overproducing yucca mutant.
source: Furthermore, in agreement with an auxin-dependent control of PIN phosphorylation at S4 and S5, we detected increased phosphorylation at S4 and S5 in the auxin-overproducing yucca mutant (Figure 10A,B, Figure 10—figure supplements 1–4; Zhao et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 10 and related supplements.

claim: The relative increases in phosphosite phosphorylations in yucca exceed the increases in overall PIN abundance.
source: Although the analyses of the control peptides showed that there is also an overall increase in PIN abundance in yucca, the relative increases in phosphosite phosphorylations exceeded the increases in overall PIN abundance suggesting that PIN phosphorylation is activated in this mutant when compared to the wild type.
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data shown in Figure 10 and related supplements.

claim: PIN phosphorylation is activated in the yucca mutant when compared to the wild type.
source: Although the analyses of the control peptides showed that there is also an overall increase in PIN abundance in yucca, the relative increases in phosphosite phosphorylations exceeded the increases in overall PIN abundance suggesting that PIN phosphorylation is activated in this mutant when compared to the wild type.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SRM analysis data.

claim: PIN1 S4 phosphorylation is strongly decreased minutes after BFA treatment when D6PK has become dissociated from the plasma membrane.
source: Importantly, we found that PIN1 S4 phosphorylation was strongly decreased already minutes after BFA treatment when D6PK had become dissociated from the plasma membrane (Figure 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 11.

claim: PIN1 S4 phosphorylation depends on the presence of D6PK or other BFA-sensitive protein kinases at the plasma membrane.
source: Thus, PIN1 S4 phosphorylation depended on the presence of D6PK or other BFA-sensitive protein kinases at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BFA treatment experiments.

claim: d6pk mutants are impaired in basipetal auxin transport in inflorescence stems.
source: In this study, we examined the functional roles of the D6PK protein kinases in PIN phosphorylation and auxin transport activation. We showed that d6pk mutants are impaired in basipetal auxin transport in inflorescence stems
evidence: This claim is supported by auxin transport measurements presented in the study.

claim: The decreases in auxin transport in inflorescence stems are not the consequence of changes in PIN abundance.
source: Furthermore, we could rule out that the decreases in auxin transport as measured in inflorescence stems are the consequence of changes in PIN abundance as demonstrated using confocal imaging, immunoblotting, and SRM analyses of PIN proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging, immunoblotting, and SRM analyses.

claim: D6PK-dependent PIN activation is dependent on specific phosphosites in PIN1 and PIN3.
source: We furthermore demonstrated that D6PK-dependent PIN activation was dependent on specific phosphosites in PIN1 and PIN3.
evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assays with phosphosite mutants.

claim: D6PKs are major regulators of PIN-mediated auxin transport in inflorescence stems.
source: Taken together, all our findings support the conclusion that D6PKs are major regulators of PIN-mediated auxin transport in inflorescence stems.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: d6pk mutant phenotypes such as gravitropism defects in the root, negative gravitropism defects in the hypocotyl, phototropism defects in the hypocotyl and defects in lateral root initiation are also the consequence of reduced auxin transport activity of PINs.
source: Since d6pk mutants have a number of phenotypes such as gravitropism defects in the root, negative gravitropism defects in the hypocotyl, phototropism defects in the hypocotyl as well as defects in lateral root initiation (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Willige et al., 2013; Barbosa et al., 2014), we are tempted to speculate that these other d6pk mutant phenotypes are also the consequence of reduced auxin transport activity of PINs in the absence of the PIN-activating D6PK kinases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the cause of d6pk mutant phenotypes.

claim: PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 and S5 are major target sites for D6PK.
source: The detailed analysis of the S1–S5 phosphosites in in vitro phosphorylation experiments and in oocyte auxin transport experiments revealed that PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 and S5 are major target sites for D6PK.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and oocyte auxin transport experiments.

claim: The preferential D6PK phosphosites S4 and S5 are not conserved in PIN2.
source: Interestingly, the preferential D6PK phosphosites S4 and S5 are not conserved in PIN2 and it is striking that the respective domains in PIN2 carry small insertions when compared to the other PIN proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The activation of PINs by phosphorylation may be regulated by the presence and abundance of activating kinases such as D6PK but also by the availability and conservation of phosphosites in their PIN targets.
source: Thus, the activation of PINs by phosphorylation may be regulated by the presence and abundance of activating kinases such as D6PK but also by the availability and conservation of phosphosites in their PIN targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phosphosite conservation analysis.

claim: PINs must have other phosphosites that are targeted by D6PK besides S4 and S5.
source: Besides S4 and S5, PINs must have other phosphosites that are targeted by D6PK since auxin transport defects in pin mutants expressing the respective PIN S4A and S5A mutant variants are partially complemented and not as severe as those observed in the d6pk012 loss-of-function mutants.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the partial complementation of pin mutants by S4A and S5A variants.

claim: D6PK has a preference for the S4 and S5 sites in PIN1 and PIN3.
source: Whereas D6PK appeared to have a preference for the S4 and S5 sites in PIN1 and PIN3, PID preferentially phosphorylated the previously identified S1–S3 phosphosites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and mass spectrometry data.

claim: PID preferentially phosphorylates the S1–S3 phosphosites.
source: Whereas D6PK appeared to have a preference for the S4 and S5 sites in PIN1 and PIN3, PID preferentially phosphorylated the previously identified S1–S3 phosphosites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and mass spectrometry data.

claim: S1–S3 are highly related to each other and also highly conserved among all five plasma membrane-resident PIN auxin efflux carriers including PIN2.
source: S1–S3 are highly related to each other and also highly conserved among all five plasma membrane-resident PIN auxin efflux carriers including PIN2.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The phosphorylation of S1–S3 contributes to full PIN phosphorylation and activation by D6PK.
source: Although D6PK had a preference for S4 and S5 phosphorylation, our in vitro phosphorylation experiments as well as the auxin transport experiments in oocytes further suggested that the phosphorylation of S1–S3 also contributes to full PIN phosphorylation and activation by D6PK.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and oocyte auxin transport experiments.

claim: Full impairment of phosphorylation and activation by PID can only be achieved after S4 mutation.
source: Whereas PID phosphorylation and activation of PIN1 was strongly impaired when S1–S3 were mutated, full impairment of phosphorylation and activation could only be achieved after S4 mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and oocyte auxin transport experiments.

claim: PIN1 S4 is not the only phosphosite required for D6PK-dependent PIN1 activation and basipetal auxin transport.
source: The partial complementation of the pin1 auxin transport defect indicates that PIN1 S4 is not the only phosphosite required for D6PK-dependent PIN1 activation and basipetal auxin transport.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the partial complementation of pin1 by PIN1 S4A.

claim: The essential phosphosites required for PID-dependent PIN activation and PIN polarity changes are retained in PIN1 S4A.
source: As shown in the in vitro phosphorylation experiment as well as in the oocyte auxin transport experiment, the PIN1 S4A mutant variant is neither strongly impaired in its phosphorylation by PID nor in its activation by PID. Thus, the essential phosphosites required for PID-dependent PIN activation and PIN polarity changes are retained in PIN1 S4A.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphorylation and oocyte auxin transport experiments.

claim: Phosphorylation at S4 and S5 is important for PIN3 activation but other phosphosites, such as S1–S3, may also be targeted by D6PK.
source: Our observation that the PIN3 S4A S5A transgene could only partially rescue the pin347 triple mutant phenotype supports the notion that phosphorylation at these sites is important for PIN3 activation but suggests further that other phosphosites, such as S1–S3, may also be targeted by D6PK.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the partial complementation of pin347 by PIN3 S4A S5A.

claim: PIN phosphorylation led to a direct activation of auxin efflux in oocytes.
source: In our experiments, PIN phosphorylation led to a direct activation of auxin efflux in oocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by oocyte auxin efflux assay data.

claim: The primary function of PIN phosphorylation is the activation of auxin transport.
source: The analysis of auxin transport in Arabidopsis inflorescence stems suggested that this might indeed be the primary function of this modification since auxin transport was strongly impaired in d6pk loss-of-function mutants while PIN abundance at the plasma membrane was not altered.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from auxin transport and PIN abundance data.

claim: PIN phosphorylation may have other regulatory roles such as control of PIN polarity by PID or WAG-dependent phosphorylation.
source: This observation does, however, not rule out that PIN phosphorylation has other regulatory roles such control of PIN polarity by PID or WAG-dependent phosphorylation (Friml et al., 2004; Dhonukshe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging other known functions of PIN phosphorylation.

claim: Changes in PIN polarity are observed after PID or WAG2 overexpression but not after D6PK overexpression.
source: Changes in PIN polarity as they are observed after PID or WAG2 overexpression are not observed after D6PK overexpression (Zourelidou et al., 2009; Dhonukshe et al., 2010; Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The differential effect of D6PK and PID/WAGs on PIN may have its molecular basis in the differential phosphosite preferences of the two kinases.
source: The differential effect of D6PK and PID/WAGs on PIN may have its molecular basis in the differential phosphosite preferences of the two kinases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the molecular basis of functional differences.

claim: The phosphorylation activity of both D6PK and PID/WAGs is antagonistically regulated by phosphatases.
source: Common to both kinases seems, however, the fact that their phosphorylation activity is antagonistically regulated by phosphatases.
evidence: This is a statement based on observations about phosphatase regulation.

claim: The phenotypic effects of PID can be antagonized by PP2A phosphatases.
source: While the phenotypic effects of PID can be antagonized by PP2A phosphatases (Michniewicz et al., 2007), removal of the D6PK from the plasma membrane through BFA treatment resulted in an almost immediate decrease in PIN1 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Removal of D6PK from the plasma membrane through BFA treatment results in an almost immediate decrease in PIN1 phosphorylation.
source: While the phenotypic effects of PID can be antagonized by PP2A phosphatases (Michniewicz et al., 2007), removal of the D6PK from the plasma membrane through BFA treatment resulted in an almost immediate decrease in PIN1 phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by BFA treatment experiments.

claim: D6PK-dependent PIN phosphorylation is antagonized by phosphatases.
source: Thus, it can be speculated that also D6PK-dependent PIN phosphorylation is antagonized by phosphatases, the identities of which remain to be determined.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the rapid dephosphorylation observed after BFA treatment.

claim: PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation is controlled by the presence of D6PK at the plasma membrane.
source: Our data also suggest that PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation is not only controlled by the presence of D6PK at the plasma membrane but also by auxin itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from BFA treatment experiments.

claim: PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation is controlled by auxin.
source: Our data also suggest that PIN1 and PIN3 phosphorylation is not only controlled by the presence of D6PK at the plasma membrane but also by auxin itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from auxin treatment experiments.

claim: PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 and S5 phosphorylation increases in response to auxin treatment in the wild type.
source: Using quantitative SRM analyses, we could show that PIN1 S4 as well as PIN3 S4 and S5 phosphorylation increases in response to auxin treatment in the wild type.
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data.

claim: The loss of phosphorylation at the preferential D6PK phosphosites in d6pk012 mutants cannot be compensated by auxin application.
source: In the d6pk012 mutant, the loss of phosphorylation at these preferential D6PK phosphosites could not be compensated by auxin application suggesting that these auxin-dependent phosphorylations are D6PK-dependent and may be mediated either directly by D6PK or by D6PK acting as an indirect auxiliary factor.
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data.

claim: Auxin-dependent phosphorylations at S4 and S5 are D6PK-dependent and may be mediated either directly by D6PK or by D6PK acting as an indirect auxiliary factor.
source: In the d6pk012 mutant, the loss of phosphorylation at these preferential D6PK phosphosites could not be compensated by auxin application suggesting that these auxin-dependent phosphorylations are D6PK-dependent and may be mediated either directly by D6PK or by D6PK acting as an indirect auxiliary factor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the auxin treatment experiments in d6pk012 mutants.

claim: The auxin-dependent increases in PIN phosphorylation may be the consequence of the inhibitory effects of auxin on PIN endocytosis.
source: Theoretically, it could be envisioned that the auxin-dependent increases in PIN phosphorylation are the consequence of the previously reported inhibitory effects of auxin on PIN endocytosis (Paciorek et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: PIN phosphorylating kinases would encounter their PIN targets for a longer period of time if auxin inhibits PIN endocytosis, thereby increasing the chances for phosphorylation.
source: In this case, PIN phosphorylating kinases would encounter their PIN targets simply for a longer period of time thereby increasing the chances for phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: Auxin treatment leads to a transient dissociation of D6PK from the plasma membrane in root cells.
source: We recently reported that auxin treatment led to a transient dissociation of D6PK from the plasma membrane in root cells There, this auxin response correlates with a slight decrease in PIN1 phosphorylation as judged by immunoblots (Barbosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Auxin promotes PIN phosphorylation in inflorescence stems.
source: In contrast, we report here that auxin promotes PIN phosphorylation in inflorescence stems as determined by quantitative mass spectrometry of PIN1 S4, PIN3 S4 and PIN3 S5.
evidence: This claim is supported by SRM analysis data.

claim: PIN phosphorylation is controlled by different auxin-dependent regulatory mechanisms in different tissues.
source: We can therefore only argue that PIN phosphorylation is controlled by different auxin-dependent regulatory mechanisms in different tissues.
evidence: This is a speculative statement to reconcile contrasting observations.

claim: PIN-mediated auxin efflux requires activation by PIN phosphorylating kinases such as D6PK and PID/WAGs.
source: In summary, our study provides evidence that PIN-mediated auxin efflux requires activation by PIN phosphorylating kinases such as D6PK and PID/WAGs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: D6PK and PID/WAGs have differential biochemical activity on PINs.
source: Several of our findings point at a differential biochemical activity of these two AGCVIII kinase representatives on PINs that may explain their differential effects in controlling PIN polarity, auxin transport, and plant growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: The differential biochemical activity of D6PK and PID/WAGs may explain their differential effects in controlling PIN polarity, auxin transport, and plant growth.
source: Several of our findings point at a differential biochemical activity of these two AGCVIII kinase representatives on PINs that may explain their differential effects in controlling PIN polarity, auxin transport, and plant growth.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional implications of differential biochemical activity.

claim: The activation of PINs by D6PKs and PID/WAGs is a crucial component of the control of auxin transport.
source: It is our view that the activation of PINs by D6PKs and PID/WAGs is a crucial component of the control of auxin transport that must be taken into account to understand auxin transport within the plant and to ultimately understand plant growth.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the importance of the findings.
